newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Telephones go down as NATO patrols divided Mostar.
newsitem.headline: Telephones go down as NATO patrols divided Mostar.

text.p: Telephone lines between Croat and Moslem parts of divided Mostar went dead on Wednesday as NATO armoured cars patrolled the tense city following an outbreak of shooting and ethnic expulsions.
French, Spanish and Moroccan troops, part of the NATO-led peace Stabilisation Force (SFOR), were on the streets with their armoured vehicles and a French combat helicopter hovered over the city.

SFOR troops deployed on Tuesday to prevent an escalation of violence that started when Croats opened fire on Moslem pilgrims trying to visit a cemetery in the Croat quarter on Monday. At least one person was killed and 22 wounded.
Hundreds of Moslems gathered in a graveyard on the Moslem-controlled eastern sector on Wednesday for the funeral of the first victim of inter-ethnic violence in months.

Shortly after the shooting, the worst incident in the southern town since the war ended in 1995, Bosnian Croats evicted some 26 Moslems from their homes, mainly from an apartment building opposite the main Croat police station.
Telephone lines between Croat and Moslem-controlled sectors also went dead without explanation. Safet Orucevic, Moslem deputy mayor of Mostar, blamed it on the Croats.

In an attempt to defuse tensions, Croat and Moslem officials, including federal president Croat Kresimir Zubak and Alija Izetbegovic, Moslem chairman of Bosnia's three-member presidency, started a meeting behind closed doors in the Bosnian capital Sarajevo.

And NATO officials said NATO personnel and members of the International Police Force (IPTF) operating in the city had escorted three families back to their homes in west Mostar. The NATO officials said they planned to continue returning the expelled families on Thursday.
Croat authorities have pledged to let all those expelled return, but the IPTF said there were still no signs of their co-operation on the ground and reported more evictions had occurred on Tuesday.
Relief workers said Croat police were blocking Moslems trying to cross back into west Mostar after day trips to the east in what amounted to de facto evictions.

Valentin Coric, interior minister for Neretva county which includes Mostar, said the IPTF formed an international commission of German, French and American officials to investigate the shooting incident.

Following the announcement that they could soon return home, a group of some 50 Moslems gathered near a bridge on the Moslem side of the Neretva river, the former confrontation line dividing the city, at midday.
Elderly people and mothers with children, looking distraught, said they were told "to gather here so we could be brought across" but nothing happened.
The Croatian state news agency HINA said Moslem police and civilians had confiscated two Croat cars on the Moslem-held north-east entrance to Mostar, after harassing and beating the drivers.
HINA said another Croat car was stoned in the town near the main boulevard, the scene of fierce Croat-Moslem fighting in 1993. Neither report could be independently verified.

The violence prompted heavy criticism of Bosnian Croats and their backers in Zagreb from Western governments and international peace envoys, including German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel and U.N. human rights envoy Elisabeth Rehn.

Both urged Zagreb, seen as standing behind hard-line Bosnian Croats who seek a separate state in south-western Bosnia, to exert control over them and prevent a recurrence of attacks on Moslems in Mostar.
The United States, whose diplomacy ended a Moslem-Croat war in early 1994 and set up a shaky bi-national federation, condemned the violence and implicitly blamed the Croats.
